title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration ID cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes (model_calls_used = 301). Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%), guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidated that planning assumption and eliminated statistical headroom for the preregistered H1 (≥50% relative reduction). We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a compact post‑hoc sensitivity statement grounded in the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded operational recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All runtime outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and are cited in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into device configuration can accelerate network operations but creates operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Prior proposals and surveys increasingly recommend generate→verify→repair patterns that pair probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators/simulators as floor‑safety nets for agentic NetOps. Despite these recommendations, there are few preregistered, paired A/B experiments that (a) use a deterministically generated task bank, (b) fix a frozen validator implementation, and (c) bound automated repair attempts to support inferential claims about first‑pass misconfiguration reductions. We implement a narrowly scoped preregistered paired experiment to address this gap and to quantify, with archived evidence, what a minimal guarded pipeline (one shared LLM candidate per task, a frozen deterministic validator, and ≤1 automated repair iteration) achieves on a controlled intent→configuration task family.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey work shows promise and risk for LLM‑assisted NetOps. Recent NetOps surveys and demonstration papers document successful template synthesis and intent translation but also emphasize failure modes—hallucination, ordering errors, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain studies in clinical QA and code generation find that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; architecture proposals for NetOps commonly recommend integrating deterministic validators into agentic pipelines as a safety floor. Our study is positioned as a narrow, preregistered empirical test of one such minimal guarded pattern under controlled paired semantics and a bounded repair budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered before execution (preregistration ID cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1). Confirmatory hypotheses were H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration recorded a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 used in power calculations; that numeric assumption is reported here because it directly influences post‑hoc inference about the trial's sensitivity.

Design and pairing semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds produced by the frozen task generator. For each seed the pipeline produced a single shared initial LLM candidate that both arms observed (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). Baseline scored the shared candidate as the plain single‑shot output; guarded applied the frozen deterministic validator and, if the validator flagged violations, invoked up to one automated repair attempt. The preregistered contract fixed initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; these constraints were not changed post registration.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model was gpt-5-mini. A frozen deterministic netops validator (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implemented rule‑ and dependency‑based checks producing canonicalized ASTs, normalized configurations, and violation codes. The validator provided binary pass/fail scores for first‑pass validity according to the preregistered scoring rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation'. Repair attempts used a constrained repair adapter that produced a single repaired candidate for validator re‑evaluation. The trial recorded per‑task normalized responses, validator traces, repair traces, and per‑episode outcomes in an execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle archived with the run.

Sampling, missingness, and contamination treatment: Sampling was paired and deterministic: planned pairs = 300, planned episodes = 600. The preregistered missingness policy allowed one provider retry per failed call and specified the primary analysis treatment 'complete_pair_primary' (drop pairs only if both calls failed). Contamination checks for exact duplicates were preregistered; none triggered deterministic exclusions. Planned outputs and artifact types were enumerated in the preregistration. All model calls, provider events, and retry attempts were recorded in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair calls invoked = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no preregistered exclusions or replacements were executed. Primary outcome counts (from archived analysis artifacts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency table derived from archived paired_contingency_table.csv: n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail).

Confirmatory statistics: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired pass/fail outcomes yields p = 1.00 given the observed discordant counts (n10=1, n01=0). The absolute paired success‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) = 1/300 = 0.0033333. A paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% confidence interval for the absolute paired difference was computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and is [0.00, 0.01]; these quantities are recorded in the archived analysis artifact bundle. The single automated repair call corrected the only initially invalid baseline output (repair success = 1/1); the exact Clopper–Pearson 95% interval for this numerator/denominator is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting large uncertainty from a single event.

Post‑hoc sensitivity and interpretable limits: Because the paired estimand is driven by discordant pairs (d = n10 + n01), the maximum resolvable absolute paired difference in this run equals d / Npairs = 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Therefore, the preregistered target effect (≈+0.30 absolute, derived from assumed baseline pass 0.40 and a 50% relative reduction in fail rate) is not detectable in this dataset: the observed discordant count of one enforces a hard ceiling on possible paired differences. Intuitively, with only a single informative discordant pair the exact McNemar test cannot reject the null for large planned effects; this mechanistic sensitivity limit is visible in the archived contingency table and bootstrap CI.

Representative task diagnostics: Representative task traces (normalized candidate, validator decision, and repair trace where invoked) are archived for inspection in the analysis bundle. The single baseline failure was remediated by the repair adapter and reclassified as valid under the frozen validator; the repair trace and validator re‑evaluation artifact are archived and were used to compute repair success. Per‑task difficulty metadata (e.g., changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) were recorded at generation time and are available in the archived task manifest to enable stratified post‑hoc analysis.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The guarded pipeline remediated the single observed baseline error, demonstrating that a deterministic validator plus a single constrained automated repair iteration can correct some validator‑detected violations. However, because the baseline pass rate was far higher than the preregistered planning assumption, the run cannot provide evidence supporting the preregistered H1 (≥50% relative reduction in fail rate). The principal scientific outcome is therefore not a demonstration of a large population‑level effect but an artifact‑grounded lesson about experimental design and inferential sensitivity for NetOps confirmatory evaluations.

Design lessons and operational implications: (1) Task‑bank difficulty calibration matters: confirmatory designs that target substantial absolute improvements must ensure baseline failure prevalence leaves statistical headroom. Here the preregistered baseline = 0.40 assumption contrasted sharply with the observed ≈0.997 baseline, eliminating power to detect large preregistered effects. (2) Pairing semantics are inferentially consequential: reusing a shared initial candidate per pair increases within‑pair correlation and reduces informative discordant pairs (lower statistical information for McNemar). Researchers should preregister pairing semantics deliberately and power accordingly. (3) Repair budget design affects operational realism and estimand choice: bounding automated repair to a single iteration constrains observed repair efficacy and may underrepresent practical multi‑step repair workflows; future confirmatory studies should align repair budgets with operational expectations and with estimands focused conditionally on initial failures.

Threats to validity (summary): Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate pairing increases within‑pair correlation and reduces discordant‑pair counts, which affects test power. Construct validity: scoring used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than dynamic execution in an emulated runtime; runtime semantic effects (reachability, performance) were not measured here. External validity: synthetic task bank, limited vendor‑template scope, single model (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation limit generalization. Conclusion validity: small number of informative discordant pairs constrains inference about large preregistered effects.

Recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps experiments: (a) calibrate or adversarially augment task banks to produce a planned baseline failure prevalence commensurate with the target estimand; (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets aligned with operational deployment semantics; (c) consider estimands focused on repair efficacy conditional on initial failure when baseline rates are low; (d) where operational claims are required, couple deterministic checks with dynamic emulation/simulation to measure runtime semantics.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 paired tasks) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt-5-mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 valid configurations and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid configurations. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. We present artifact‑grounded recommendations for calibrating task difficulty, preregistering pairing semantics and repair budgets, and integrating runtime emulation when making operational readiness claims. All runtime outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and are referenced in the Disclosure Statement to support reproducibility and method refinement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.

Sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations (reachability, performance) were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
